title: Tenant Isolation
summary: Prevent one tenant’s identity, data, state, tools, or resource consumption from crossing into another tenant’s execution boundary.
overview: Tenant isolation spans the entire agent system: authentication, retrieval, caches, memory, queues, checkpoints, tools, logs, and model-serving resources. Adding a tenant column is useful only if every relevant operation enforces it. Derive tenant context from trusted identity and carry it through all asynchronous and delegated work.

Choose isolation strength from risk and operating requirements. Shared infrastructure with enforced partitions can be efficient; separate databases, keys, workers, or accounts provide stronger boundaries at greater cost. Data isolation and performance isolation are distinct: preventing cross-tenant reads does not prevent one tenant from exhausting shared capacity.

production.poc: A prototype with one tenant hides many isolation assumptions. Add two synthetic tenants with overlapping document and user identifiers before expanding access.
production.production: Production uses mandatory tenant predicates, tenant-aware cache keys, scoped credentials, and isolated session state. Background jobs must reconstruct trusted tenant context rather than use a global default.
production.scale: At scale, test migration, backup restoration, support tooling, and noisy-neighbor behavior. Isolation controls need to remain intact during administrative operations as well as ordinary requests.

components.name: Tenant identity resolver
components.role: Establishes trusted tenant context from authenticated sessions or service credentials.

components.name: Data partition layer
components.role: Enforces tenant boundaries in retrieval, records, object storage, and checkpoint access.

components.name: Execution scope
components.role: Carries tenant identity through queues, workers, delegation, and tool credentials.

components.name: Cache and memory boundary
components.role: Prevents shared keys, reused sessions, or summaries from mixing tenant content.

components.name: Resource governor
components.role: Applies tenant quotas and monitors performance interference separately from data access.

flow.title: Resolve tenant
flow.description: Bind a request to authenticated tenant context and reject conflicting user-supplied identifiers.

flow.title: Scope resources
flow.description: Select permitted partitions, keys, credentials, and execution pools.

flow.title: Propagate context
flow.description: Attach trusted tenant metadata to durable jobs and child tasks.

flow.title: Enforce access
flow.description: Apply mandatory boundaries at every data and tool service, including cache lookup.

flow.title: Publish scoped results
flow.description: Validate that artifacts and citations belong to the requesting tenant.

flow.title: Audit isolation
flow.description: Test cross-tenant requests, administrative paths, and resource contention continuously.

diagrams.title: Tenant context survives queue delivery
diagrams.code:
sequenceDiagram
 participant A as Authenticated API
 participant Q as Durable queue
 participant W as Worker
 participant S as Scoped data service
 A->>A: Resolve trusted tenant identity
 A->>Q: Persist job with verified tenant context
 Q->>W: Deliver job and context
 W->>W: Validate scope and claim ownership
 W->>S: Read using tenant-scoped credentials
 S-->>W: Authorized tenant records
 W->>S: Store artifact with tenant ownership
diagrams.caption: The worker reconstructs trusted scope and cannot substitute a global default when metadata is missing.

useCase.title: Separating building-owner portfolios
useCase.situation: A SaaS platform offers maintenance assistants to property owners with separate tenants and overlapping contractor names.
useCase.problem: A cache keyed only by a natural-language question can return another owner's maintenance history.
useCase.requirement: The assistant must isolate portfolio records, conversations, work orders, and generated reports while sharing infrastructure efficiently.
useCase.architecture: Trusted tenant context scopes database rows, vector partitions, cache keys, worker jobs, and contractor-tool credentials.
runtime: A manager asks about recurring elevator failures; retrieval and cache lookup are restricted to that owner's portfolio.
The generated report and its download route retain tenant ownership and recheck it on access.
useCase.failure: If a background job lacks tenant context, it fails before retrieving data instead of falling back to an application-wide credential.
useCase.impact: Measure cross-tenant test failures, missing-scope rejections, cache isolation, and noisy-neighbor latency under concurrent load.

tradeoffs.benefit: Capacity and operating costs are easier to pool.
tradeoffs.cost: Every shared layer needs reliable enforcement.

tradeoffs.benefit: Boundaries and capacity guarantees become stronger.
tradeoffs.cost: Provisioning, upgrades, and utilization become more expensive.

tradeoffs.benefit: Cryptographic separation supports stronger data control.
tradeoffs.cost: Key lifecycle and recovery require additional operations.

failures.scenario: A reused agent session retains prior tenant context
failures.detection: Isolation tests find another tenant's artifact references in memory.
failures.recovery: Destroy the session and enforce tenant-bound reuse rules.

failures.scenario: A support tool bypasses normal filters
failures.detection: Administrative audit reveals unrestricted access paths.
failures.recovery: Add explicit scoped access and auditable exceptional procedures.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting tenant IDs in request text
Isolating the database but sharing cache keys
mistakes.fix: Include tenant and authorization scope across all derived stores.
Test isolation through administrative data movement.

whenToUse: One platform serves independent customer organizations.
Data and operational boundaries differ by tenant.
Shared resources need both access and fairness controls.
whenNotToUse: The application is intentionally single-tenant and isolated already.
Tenant identity cannot be established reliably.
Shared deployment cannot meet required boundary strength.
